questions.question: Which exact board do you have? The pin maps and onboard peripherals differ between the variants, and getting this wrong means a black screen.

options.label: ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-4.3 (plain)
options.description: The standard 800×480 board: RGB panel, GT911 touch, CH422G expander, SD slot, CAN + RS485 headers, PH2.0 battery connector. This is what my research above is based on.

options.label: ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-4.3B
options.description: The 'B' revision — same panel and touch, but a different board layout with an onboard RTC, extra sensor headers, and some GPIO reassignments. I'd re-verify the pin table against the 4.3B docs before writing board.h.

options.label: Not sure — I'll check the silkscreen
options.description: I can also have you run a quick esptool/I2C scan once it's plugged in to fingerprint it (flash size, PSRAM type, which I2C addresses ACK).

questions.question: With no readable physical button, how should the 4.3 handle the HID keyboard features (Space for Claude Code voice-mode push-to-talk, Shift+Tab for mode toggle)?

options.label: On-screen soft buttons (Recommended)
options.description: Add a touch control strip to the usage screen with PTT + mode-toggle buttons, shown only when board_caps().button_count == 0. Keeps the headline HID feature, and 800×480 has room to spare. Cost: a gated addition to shared ui.cpp — the first port that adds UI rather than just re-laying it out.

options.label: Touch-only, drop HID
options.description: Simplest possible port: no keyboard at all. Tap toggles splash ↔ usage (already works via global_click_cb), long-press somewhere enters pairing. The 4.3 becomes a pure display. Zero changes to shared code beyond a layout breakpoint.

options.label: Solder an external button
options.description: GPIO 6 (and 43/44 if you don't need UART0) appear free on the headers. Wire a momentary button to GND and the port keeps a real physical PTT key exactly like the other boards. Requires soldering and I'd want you to meter the pin first.

questions.question: The next thing to settle is how the UI fills an 800×480 landscape screen — every existing port is square or portrait, so this is a genuinely visual call. I can spin up a browser tab and show you real mockups and side-by-side comparisons as we go instead of describing them in ASCII. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to open it?

options.label: No — keep it in the terminal
options.description: I'll describe the layout options with ASCII sketches and we'll do the real visual iteration on hardware later via screenshot.sh, which is how the other ports were tuned anyway. Faster and cheaper.

options.label: Yes — open the visual companion
options.description: I'll start the companion server and your browser opens to rendered 800×480 mockups you can compare directly. Better fidelity for the layout decision, more tokens.

questions.question: How should the usage screen use the 800×480 landscape space?

options.label: Two-column landscape (Recommended)
options.description: New breakpoint keyed on a wide aspect ratio: headline percentage + bar on the left, secondary detail and the TALK/MODE buttons on the right. Uses the whole panel and reads well from across a desk. Most layout work, best result — and it's the branch a future 800×480 porter would inherit.

options.label: Centered 480-wide column
options.description: Reuse the existing 'large' 480×480 layout verbatim, centered horizontally with 160 px of background either side. Almost no new layout code — lowest risk, fastest to a working screen. Wastes 40% of the panel and will look like a phone app on a monitor.

options.label: Full-width single column
options.description: Keep the existing vertical stacking but let panels and bars span the full 800 px. Minimal code (widen content_w, add the button row). Bars become very long and the existing fonts will look small against all that width — sparse but honest, and easy to refine later on hardware.

questions.question: The 4.3's backlight is a single on/off line on the CH422G expander (EXIO2 → DISP), so display_hal_set_brightness() can't do the smooth 0–255 fade the AMOLED boards do. How should idle-dimming and the brightness-cycle feature behave?

options.label: Hybrid: LVGL scrim + hard blank (Recommended)
options.description: Map brightness levels to a full-screen black overlay whose opacity varies (real perceived dimming, backlight stays on), and let the deep idle timeout actually cut EXIO2 so the panel goes dark and saves power. Touch wakes it. Keeps both features feeling like the other boards; the scrim lives in the board's display.cpp, not shared code.

options.label: Binary only
options.description: set_brightness() becomes a threshold: anything above ~10 turns the backlight on, below turns it off. Idle timeout blanks the screen, touch wakes it. brightness_cycle() becomes a no-op or an on/off toggle. Simplest and most honest to the hardware; no gradual fade.

options.label: Always on
options.description: Never touch EXIO2 after boot — backlight permanently on, no idle blanking, no brightness cycling. Fewest moving parts, but a desk-side display glowing at full brightness all night and no power saving on battery.
